name: Daria Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small independent garage that mostly does hybrids and electric cars, in an old railway arch near the canal. First thing I check the overnight messages, then I'm usually on battery health checks, brake jobs, the odd inverter fault on a taxi. I use an AI assistant all day, honestly, to read fault logs, compare wiring diagrams and draft the explanation for the customer. The bit I love is a weird electrical fault that three other garages gave up on; the bit that drains me is lifting batteries in a cramped bay with my back complaining.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who runs the place, and how did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mo owns it; he's in his forties and was smart enough to go electric early. I came from a big chain where I did tyres and services for five years and was bored stiff. I share a flat with my friend Tess, who's a nurse, and I've got about two and a half months saved, which I keep meaning to grow. My dream, if I'm honest, is a co-op garage one day, owned by the people who work in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, if anything. I'd post that AI turned out to be a nice spanner, not a new workshop. At work I'd tell Mo we got our money's worth from the subscription anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good news for me. Electric cars keep coming in, there aren't many people who can safely work on them, and Mo's booked out three weeks ahead. My job looks solid, so it's really just about rent and growing my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and push to get more certified on high-voltage systems, level four maybe, so I'm the person garages call. I'd up my savings to 300 a month. I'd start talking to Tess's cousin, who's an accountant, about how co-ops actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I like change, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the subscription was worth it. What does the AI actually save you in a day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About an hour, I'd guess. It reads a fault log in seconds that used to take me twenty minutes with a coffee. That hour goes into the next car, so Mo's happy and I go home on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a co-op, rather than your own garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what happens when one owner calls every shot and then retires or sells. A co-op means the people doing the work decide where it goes. It's slower to set up, but it lasts.

say: I'd post that AI turned out to be **a nice spanner**, not a new workshop.
I'd tell Mo the **AI subscription** paid for itself anyway.
think: The plateau is **good news** for me, with electric work booked weeks ahead.
My job looks **solid**, so rent and growing savings are my only real concerns.
do: Get **level four** high-voltage certification to become the go-to specialist.
Raise savings to **300 a month** from the current two and a half months.
Ask an **accountant** how worker co-ops are set up.
feel: **Calm**, if slightly flat, because she enjoys change.
S0.quote: AI turned out to be a nice spanner, not a new workshop.
fieldNote: Already a **daily AI user**; the plateau changes nothing for her.
Security comes from **scarce electric skills**, not from AI.
The **co-op dream** reflects her politics and distrust of single owners.

steps.text: Get level four high-voltage certification for electric car work
Keep working the electric car bookings at Mo's garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be good for some of us and rough for loads of people, so we need proper support for the ones it hits. I'd post about free retraining and a shorter working week. I'd say it in the pub too, and probably start an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd do all right. The thinking side of my job is already half AI, and the hands-on electric work is the slow bit robots won't touch for a while. What bothers me is my old mates at the chain, where the booking, the upsells and the service reminders are exactly what AI eats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the tools, and I'd offer to set them up for other small garages on Saturdays, for a fee. I'd keep the savings going and start properly meeting people who might want to do a co-op with me. And I'd join the union, mostly for the people I left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit excited, a bit guilty. Mostly uneasy about how other people land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who from your old chain would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who I trained with. He's brilliant at talking customers into new tyres, and that's the job an AI chatbot does now. He doesn't have savings and he's got a baby on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd set up AI tools for other garages. Is that a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could be a small one. Plenty of old-school garages have no idea where to start, and I can do it in a morning. Fifty quid a garage, a few a month, and that's my savings doubled.

say: I'd say people hit by AI need **proper support**, like free retraining.
I'd post about a **shorter working week** and argue it in the pub.
think: I'd do **all right**, since my thinking work is already half AI.
My old chain's **booking and upsell** jobs are exactly what AI eats.
do: Set up AI tools for **other small garages** on Saturdays for fifty pounds each.
Meet people seriously interested in starting a **co-op garage**.
Join the **union** to support workers she left behind.
feel: **Excited and guilty** at once, uneasy about how others will land.
S1.quote: The thinking side of my job is already half AI, and the hands-on electric work is the slow bit robots won't touch for a while.
fieldNote: Accurately splits her job into **thinking and hands-on** parts.
Her worry is for **Dev**, an old colleague with a baby coming and no savings.
Turns her AI skill into a **Saturday side income** straight away.

steps.text: Set up AI tools for small garages on Saturdays at fifty pounds each
Hold meetings with mechanics interested in a co-op garage
Join the union to support workers at her old chain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a universal basic income, a monthly payment for everyone, and we need it this year. I'd be online every night about it. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the first two years I'm fine, because AGI makes me faster, not jobless. But by 2031 a robot that can lift a battery and follow an AI's instructions does my job without a sore back. I'd be thirty-two and back to square one, just with better stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze everything out of those three years: work extra hours, save 500 a month, and put it toward a co-op that runs robots rather than fights them. I'd get trained on robot maintenance as early as anyone offers it. And I'd move somewhere cheaper if the rent went up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing as well. Like being on a fast road with no map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a co-op that runs robots. What does that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Instead of a robot company owning the machines and selling the service, a group of mechanics owns the robots together, and we share what the robots earn. We'd still be the people who know cars. It's a long shot, but it's better than waiting to be replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to get to 500 a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, the gym, and the car I don't really need since I live by the canal. I'd sell my old Golf and cycle. That's three hundred a month on its own.

say: I'd demand a **basic income**, a monthly payment for everyone, this year.
I'd be **online every night** pushing it to anyone who'd listen.
think: Until 2031 AGI makes me **faster, not jobless**.
By **2031** a robot following AI instructions does my work without a sore back.
do: Save **500 a month** by working extra hours and cutting costs.
Sell the **old Golf** and cycle to work instead.
Pool money into a **co-op that owns robots** with other mechanics.
feel: **Anxious but buzzing**, like a fast road with no map.
S2.quote: A group of mechanics owns the robots together, and we share what the robots earn.
fieldNote: She precisely uses the **three-year window** before robots to save and build.
Answer to automation is **ownership**, not resistance.
Mixed feelings: fear of 2031 and real **excitement** now.

steps.text: Save 500 a month by working extra hours at the garage
Sell the old Golf and cycle to work
Put savings into a mechanics' co-op that owns robot equipment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set things up properly, if people stop pretending it's not coming. I'd push for training money and co-op start-up loans. Online, at work, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one suits me. I'd be thirty-two when AGI lands and thirty-five when the robots come, with a few years of savings and a business partly built. Five years is just enough time to go from mechanic to owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year finding three or four people for the co-op and getting a business loan. I'd keep working at Mo's, keep the Saturday AI setups going, and learn robot maintenance before 2034. Maybe Mo would even join us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Mostly hopeful, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mo really join a co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might, actually. He's tired, and he once said he'd love to hand the paperwork to someone else. If we offered to buy him in, he'd keep the arch and stop worrying about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plan fall apart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. If the banks won't lend to a co-op, I'm stuck with my own savings, which is a few months' rent. That's the bit that keeps me up.

say: I'd say five years is enough if people **stop pretending**.
I'd push for **training money** and start-up loans for co-ops.
think: This scenario **suits me**: five years to go from mechanic to owner.
I'd have savings and a **business partly built** by the time robots come.
do: Recruit **three or four people** for the co-op in year one.
Apply for a **business loan** while staying on at Mo's.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough time to go from mechanic to owner.
fieldNote: The five-year window makes her **ambitious**, not afraid.
Main risk she names is **lending to a co-op**.
Hopes to bring **Mo, the owner**, into the plan.

steps.text: Recruit three or four mechanics for the co-op in year one
Apply for a business loan for the co-op garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. Build training into schools and colleges now. Make sure the companies that profit pay into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands and forty when the robots come. By then I'd hope to be running the co-op, not working under the robots. This is the version where I mostly win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it slower: get the co-op running in five years, not two. I'd keep learning every new AI tool as it appears. I'd probably teach evening classes at the college on electric cars too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Calm and a bit impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mostly win. Who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anyone who spends the ten years pretending, and people who can't afford to retrain because they've got kids and rent. My mum's like that; she works at a call centre. I'd want to help her plan more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Evening classes. Why teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learned from an old mechanic who took time with me, and there's hardly anyone teaching electric cars. It'd pay a bit too. And it keeps me close to the young people coming through.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift we'd be idiots to waste.
I'd call for **training in colleges** now, paid for by companies that profit.
think: This is the version where **I mostly win**.
By forty I'd hope to be **running the co-op**, not working under robots.
do: Build the **co-op** over five years instead of rushing it.
Teach **evening classes** on electric cars at the college.
Keep learning each **new AI tool** as it appears.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it.
fieldNote: Long warning gives her **confidence**; she plans to own, not be replaced.
Her worry moves to **her mum** at a call centre.
Teaching repays the **old mechanic** who trained her.

steps.text: Launch the co-op garage within five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't enough to build anything, and I'd be scrambling. What would help is cheap loans for worker co-ops and real training on robots before they arrive, not after. And a basic income so people like my mum aren't left on their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if robots take the jobs, but nobody asks who gets paid when they do. If the mechanics own the robots, AGI is a pay rise; if a tech company owns them, it's a P45.

headlineQuote: If the mechanics own the robots, AGI is a pay rise; if a tech company owns them, it's a P45.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old electric car specialist** at a small garage in a railway arch.
She uses **AI every day** and dreams of a worker-owned co-op garage.
Progressive, she asks **who owns the robots** rather than whether they come.
She stays **calm or uneasy** in most scenarios, anxious only when AGI comes in two years.
Her worry often turns to **others**: an old colleague, her mum at a call centre.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years before robots isn't enough to build the co-op.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for worker co-ops and early training on robot maintenance.
A **basic income** so people like her mum aren't left alone.
